newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Black empowerment mirrors Afrikaner struggle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Black empowerment mirrors Afrikaner struggle.

text.p: After decades of exclusion an oppressed people wins political power in South Africa and forces open barred doors to the economy.
A story of the anti-apartheid struggle and black empowerment?

It looks that way, but for white Afrikaners -- who set up the racist apartheid system that ruled South Africa for more than 40 years -- it also describes their own fight against the rule of Britain and English-speaking whites.

"There are a lot of similarities. The domination of the English in the business environment was too big and the Afrikaner people felt excluded," said Geoff Hlabangane, chairman of black oil firm Naledi Petroleum Industries.
Black empowerment is in vogue in the new South Africa that emerged after the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
Companies are scrambling to bring in black partners and the economic muscle of those who just three years ago could not vote is growing stronger by the day.
But Afrikaners, in their struggle for power after losing the Anglo-Boer war of 1899-1902, pioneered South Africa's first empowerment process.
BLACKS AND AFRIKANERS: NATURAL ALLIES?
Some industry-watchers even believe this shared experience may form the seeds of a seemingly unlikely partnership between blacks and their former oppressors.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Gordon Smith says the parallel empowerment experiences of blacks and Afrikaners gives the two some common ground.
They also often share a more upfront style of business culture compared to the more reserved English-speakers. "Anglos can be just too diplomatic," he said.
Hlabangane agrees.

"We found a lot of willingness and honesty in terms of facilitating black empowerment (from Afrikaner businesses). There is a natural understanding between black empowerment and Afrikaner business," he said.

Under the twin blows of losing the fight against Britain and rural depression after World War One, Afrikaners banded together to form their own companies and banks aimed at hitting back at the English-speaking white-dominated economy.
Current giants such as mutual life assurer Sanlam, the main vehicle for Afrikaner economic empowerment, have their roots in this movement.
KEY GOVERNMENT ROLE
When the Afrikaner-based National Party won power in the whites-only 1948 elections the process quickened with government favours and contracts going to Afrikaner firms.

Now the African National Congress-led government of Nelson Mandela is creating the conditions for black business to grow. "Government has provided the enabling political and social environment," Smith said.
A seminal deal for the Afrikaners created Gencor in 1964 when Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd supported small Afrikaner mining house Federale Mynbou's takeover of General Mining.
In mineral rich South Africa control of a mining house -- long the preserve of English-speaking whites -- is the final sign that an ethnic group has arrived in political power.
Now it is the turn of blacks.

Less than three years on from the election they have already won control of the sixth largest mining house, JCI Ltd, following another sale by Anglo -- this time to black consortium African Mining Group.
In 1992 there were only five black-run companies on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) with a market capitalisation of 1.8 billion rand. In 1996 the figure was 17 firms worth 26.5 billion rand.

Some of the key deals in this process have been struck with Afrikaner businesses, such as those in the early 1990s that gave black empowerment group New Africa Investments Ltd control over insurer Metropolitan Life Ltd.

Even the pillars of the old apartheid state are joining in. Sasol Ltd, whose oil-from-coal technology was an effective sanctions buster in the years of economic isolation, has joined up with Naledi Petroleum and is hunting for another black partner in its downstream chemicals business.
BLACK EMPOWERMENT QUICKER

But black empowerment has occurred much more quickly than its Afrikaner counterpart and involves a much larger section of the population which previously had been almost totally excluded in a way Afrikaners never were.
Its effects will therefore be much deeper.

"Black empowerment is going to be done on an even larger and more massive scale then the Afrikaners," said Emmanuel Lediga, managing director of the country's first black stockbroking firm Legae Securities.
Lediga, who was the first black JSE floor trader and cofounded Legae, said one of the main differences between black and Afrikaner empowerment is blacks have less access to funding.
However, with the government firmly behind the process black empowerment is here to stay and financial institutions are showing leniency in their dealings with black groups.

Lediga says hard-nosed business reasons lie behind much of the black empowerment phenomenon. But with a past so bitterly scarred by racial conflict, he believes it will take two generations before business becomes truly colour blind.
